title: Regional prefetch + graceful degradation policy for dedicated allocations
creator: Marco Liu
description:
Background: Several incidents and test runs have shown that naive spillover from Dedicated capacity -> Hosted causes opaque latency spikes and customer-visible errors when region selection and model variant compatibility are not enforced. This ticket proposes a policy and implementation that (1) prefetches capacity/variant compatibility information per-region for tenants with Dedicated allocations, (2) performs SLA-aware graded degradation before triggering cross-region or hosted spillover, and (3) enforces throttled, observable spillover with per-tenant circuit-breakers and telemetry.

Goals:
- Reduce P99 end-to-end latency regressions during capacity pressure by ensuring routing decisions prefer compatible local variants or pre-warmed remote capacity.
- Avoid silent degradations: surface a clear degraded mode for the customer when fallbacks are active.
- Limit blast radius of spillovers with tenant-scoped limits and progressive throttles.

Proposal (high level):
1) Regional prefetch table: for each tenant mark their preferred regions and maintain a cached table with per-region: available dedicated capacity, list of compatible model variants (quant/precision / kv-cache compatibility), estimated cold-start time, and last-sync timestamp. This table is updated via a low-rate poll + event hooks.
2) SLA-aware degradation sequence: when local Dedicated capacity is saturated, evaluate in order: (a) try local compatible variants with controlled concurrency, (b) try remote Dedicated in same geo (if latency budget allows), (c) try remote Dedicated with cross-region pre-warm check, (d) finally spill to Hosted but only up to an adjustable throttle and after annotating requests with a 'degraded' flag.
3) Throttles and circuit-breakers: per-tenant counters that increment on fallbacks; policy decays counters over time. When counter exceeds threshold we fail fast to a graceful 429 or a configurable degraded response instead of routing to Hosted, to avoid unbounded cost and protect model quality.
4) Model-variant compatibility matrix: a compact fingerprinting mechanism (architecture, kv-cache format, quantization variant) so runtime can quickly decide whether a remote variant is a compatible substitute without full validation.
5) Observability & rollback: add metrics and dashboards for fallback rate, per-tenant degradation score, P50/P95/P99 per routing tier, hosted spillover cost, and model-quality deltas (using recent eval prompts). Add an alert when hosted spillover > X% of requests for a tenant for > 5m.

Engineering design notes:
- Data plane: router queries the regional prefetch table (in-memory with TTL). Prefetch table is updated by a control-plane service that aggregates capacity signals from autoscaler and a lightweight compatibility probe that checks variant metadata only (no model load).
- Decision latency: routing checks must add <1ms median. Prefetch table must be highly available and sharded by tenant to avoid hot keys.
- Fallback annotation: requests routed to fallback MUST include a header/provenance token so downstream billing and quality monitoring can identify degraded responses.
- Tenant config: allow tenants to opt into "aggressive spillover" or "strict-local-only" modes; default follows SLO tier mapping.

Acceptance criteria:
- End-to-end routing decision path adds <2ms median latency for canary tenant.
- Simulated saturation test: under synthetic 3x demand spike, P99 latency for canary tenant must not exceed baseline by more than 1.5x and hosted spillover cost must be limited to the configured throttle.
- Circuit-breaker kicks in and returns controlled 429 or configurable fallback response when threshold exceeded.
- Dashboards show fallback rate, regional capacity sync latency, and per-tenant degradation score.
- Unit and integration tests covering prefetched table staleness, compatibility matrix mismatch, and circuit-breaker behavior.

Testing & rollout plan:
- Unit tests for compatibility fingerprinting and decision logic.
- Integration tests in staging with synthetic tenants and controlled dedicated capacity.
- Canary rollout to 3 low-traffic tenants for 48 hours with feature flag. Monitor: fallback_rate, P99_latency_increase, hosted_spillover_cost. If fallback_rate > 5% OR P99 increase > 2x OR cost > budget -> rollback.
- Gradual ramp to more tenants and finally default for new Dedicated allocations.

Trade-offs & open questions:
- Pull vs push for prefetch table: push reduces staleness but increases control-plane complexity. Proposed hybrid: push for critical events (capacity changes), periodic pull for reconciling missed events.
- Compatibility fingerprint granularity: too coarse -> incorrect substitutions, too fine -> many variants considered incompatible causing more spillover. Start with moderate granularity (arch + kv-cache format + quant bucket) and refine with telemetry.
- Customer-visible degradation semantics: whether to return a 429, a short-circuit cached response, or route to hosted with a banner. Default to 429 with opt-in for alternate behaviors.

Security considerations:
- Prefetch table contains tenant routing preferences and capacity metadata but no secrets. Ensure access controlled and logged. Annotated fallback tokens must not leak customer secrets and should be minimal.

Next steps:
- Review with infra and product (security & pricing) to finalize throttle defaults.
- Implement compatibility fingerprint library and unit tests (owner: Aisha).
- Instrument metrics and staged rollout plan (owner: Marco).
